O.outcome_detail: LMS login activity distribution by time of day

cells.quote: Consistent with this, women (N = 5887) exhibited significantly more activity than men (N = 7890) in the evening (18:00–24:00, F = 143, p = 6 × 10−33), while men exhibited significantly increased activity relative to women at night (00:00–6:00, F = 47, p = 9 × 10−12, Fig. 2A).
cells.note: The study used LMS login activity as a proxy for circadian timing; the contrast is observational rather than a learning intervention.

O.outcome_detail: phase of LMS login activity

result.effect: Morning activity: F = 17.05, p = 5 × 10−14; evening activity: F = 18.29, p = 5 × 10−15

cells.quote: Comparison across decades of age (10–19, N = 2323; 20–29, N = 8770; 30–39, N = 2337; 40–49, N = 910; 50+, N = 509) revealed a significantly earlier phase of morning activity (06:00–12:00, F = 17.05, p = 5 × 10−14) and evening activity (18:00–24:00: F = 18.29, p = 5 × 10−15; Fig. 2B) for each additional decade of life.
cells.note: The cohort spanned teenagers to students in their 70s, so age is coded as mixed.

O.outcome_detail: seasonal distribution of LMS login activity

cells.quote: Consistent with this expectation, in both years, the fall and spring showed significant differences (F = 10.6, p = 0.001; Fig. 2C) in login activity distribution. In the fall semesters, students exhibited increased activity in the middle of the day, consistent with the consolidation of activity under a shortening light phase. Conversely, in the spring semesters, student activity increased in the early and late day, consistent with the spreading of activity as the light phase lengthens.
cells.note: This validation contrast compares semesters across two academic years; the study interpreted the seasonal pattern as consistent with circadian timing.
